title: FAA Lifts Nationwide Ground Stop After Aging Tech Failure Triggers Sky Gridlock
snippet: A sweeping telecommunications failure halted thousands of flights across the United States on Friday, exposing critical vulnerabilities in the nation's aging air traffic infrastructure.
content:
U.S. aviation officials lifted a historic, nationwide ground stop late Friday night following a massive telecommunications breakdown that crippled air traffic control systems, grounding thousands of flights and stranding travelers across the country.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed during an evening press conference that U.S. airspace had reopened and departures were slowly resuming. However, he cautioned that clearing the immense backlog of planes would be a prolonged process.

"It’s going to take us some time to unwind what happened this afternoon," Duffy said, warning that flight operations would remain sluggish through the night.

An 'Incredibly Old System' Under Pressure

The disruption began just after 3:30 p.m. ET, when critical radar communications failed at Air Route Traffic Control Centers nationwide, instantly impacting more than 3,500 aircraft airborne at the time. Duffy attributed the catastrophic breakdown to decades of underinvestment in the nation’s flight safety infrastructure.

"We have old switches, old routers, we use 1980s little copper lines," Duffy explained. "It's an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded."

Duffy pushed Congress to authorize a $50 billion emergency modernization fund, warning that without a fundamental overhaul, future outages are inevitable. While lawmakers approved $12.5 billion last year to replace legacy infrastructure, federal officials argue far more capital is required to replace systems that haven't seen a total revamp in decades.

No Evidence of Cyberattack

Addressing heightened national security concerns, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin emphasized that there was no initial indication of foul play or a cyberattack behind the blackout.

"There is no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for their loved ones," Mullin told reporters, attempting to calm public anxiety. "This is not another 9/11. This is a telecommunications outage; this is much different."

Initial reports indicate the outage stemmed from a network update within a private telecommunications framework managed by L3Harris Technologies, which handles vital radio frequencies connecting air traffic controllers with pilots. tech giants and aviation software providers confirmed that other recent software issues were unrelated to the FAA system failure.

Travel Chaos and Calls for Investigation

By late Friday, flight-tracking platform FlightAware reported more than 6,600 flight cancellations and over 25,000 delays nationwide. Major airports were engulfed in gridlock, with thousands of passengers stranded in terminals or left waiting on tarmacs for hours.

The unprecedented freeze drew immediate reaction from lawmakers on Capitol Hill. Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-IL), ranking member of the Senate Subcommittee on Aviation, demanded a full congressional inquiry into the outage.

"The safety of our skies is built on redundancies," Duckworth said in a statement. "Whatever led to the nationwide ground stop will warrant a thorough and complete investigation."

Nationwide ground stops of this scale remain extraordinarily rare in U.S. history. The last systemic halt occurred in January 2023 due to a pilot safety database malfunction, with the only prior nationwide order occurring in the immediate aftermath of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.
